title: Tips for Anyone Using AI to Make Games 🎮 — Things I Wish More People Knew
author: Quiet-Still7844
selftext:
**The reason AI is given a bad name is because a lot of people start projects without any kind of direction, and then end up with half baked nonsense that makes it hard for the real gems that were made with AI get seen****.**  
AI tools make game development more accessible than ever, especially for those who aren’t experienced programmers, artists, or game developers. But using AI doesn’t automatically make game development easy. You still need a plan, direction, and a bit of discipline.  
Here are some tips that I think can make a huge difference when building a game with AI.  
**1. Plan your game BEFORE you start building it.**  
I know it’s tempting to jump straight into your game engine and start prompting AI to create things, but take a step back first.  
What kind of game are you making? What’s the core gameplay loop? What does the player actually do? What is the goal? What are the essential mechanics? a simple outline of your idea, the core mechanics, and your first few milestones is better than starting with no direction.  
**2. Keep a project notebook. Seriously.**   
This is one of the most underrated things you can do when working with AI.  
Keep a notebook or a project document where you record:  
Your original game concept and vision.  
Planned features and mechanics.  
Decisions you’ve made and WHY you made them.  
Your folder structure, scripts, and how different systems connect.  
Bugs you’ve encountered and how you fixed them.  
What currently works, what doesn’t, and what needs to happen next.  
AI can help you build things, but you need a reliable record of your project’s direction. This becomes especially important when you’re working across multiple conversations or switching between AI tools. Don’t rely on the AI to remember everything.  
**3. Prioritise PLAYABILITY over visuals.**  
This is a big one!  
Don’t spend three days perfecting the grass textures, character designs, lighting, or UI before you’ve even confirmed that the game is fun to play.  
Start with basic shapes, placeholder sprites, simple environments, and ugly prototypes if necessary.  
Can the player move? Do the mechanics work? Is the core gameplay loop enjoyable? Does the game feel responsive?  
Get those things right FIRST. You can make everything beautiful later. A gorgeous game that isn’t fun to play is still a problem.  
**4. Build small features, one at a time.**  
Avoid asking AI to build your entire game in one giant prompt. The more complex the request, the harder it becomes to identify what went wrong when something breaks.  
Instead, break the project into manageable tasks. For example:  
First, get player movement working.  
Then add interaction with objects.  
Next, add inventory functionality.  
Then introduce saving and loading.  
Test each feature before moving on. Small, working systems are much easier to maintain than one enormous collection of AI-generated code.  
**5. Don’t blindly trust AI-generated code.**  
AI can produce code that looks convincing but contains bugs, makes incorrect assumptions, or breaks something that was already working.  
Run the game frequently. Read the error messages. Test edge cases. Ask the AI to explain what a script does before accepting changes you don’t understand.  
You don’t have to be an expert programmer, but you should gradually learn enough to understand the systems you’re building.  
**6. Give your AI clear context.**  
Instead of saying, “Make me an inventory system,” explain your game engine, programming language, existing systems, desired behaviour, and any constraints.  
For example: “I’m using Godot 4 with GDScript. My player already has an interaction system. Create an inventory that integrates with it without rewriting the existing movement or interaction scripts.”  
The more relevant context you provide, the less likely you are to get a solution that doesn’t fit your project.  
**7. Use version control and backups.**  
Before making major changes, create a backup or commit your working version to Git.  
AI can accidentally overwrite working code, restructure files, or introduce bugs while fixing something else. Having a known-good version means you can recover instead of starting over.  
**8. Don’t keep adding features before finishing the basics.**  
It’s easy to fall into the trap of constantly adding new ideas. You start with a farming game, then add fishing, cooking, crafting, pets, relationships, multiplayer, and a massive open world.  
Suddenly, you have 50 unfinished systems and nothing that feels complete.  
Get a small playable version working first. Finish a tiny slice of your game before expanding it.  
**9. Treat AI as a collaborator, not a replacement for your judgement.**  
AI is a tool. You are still the game designer.  
You decide what makes your game unique, which suggestions fit your vision, what needs improving, and what should be removed. Don’t let the AI make every design decision simply because it can generate something quickly.  
**10. Test the actual game, not just whether the code runs.**  
A script can run without errors and the game can still feel terrible.  
Play through your game as a player would. Try unusual inputs, repeat actions, explore the limits of mechanics, and look for confusing interactions. If possible, let someone else try it without explaining how everything works.  
The goal isn’t just to make code that works. It’s to make an experience people enjoy.

**My biggest takeaway:** AI makes it easier to create things, but it doesn’t remove the need for planning, testing, and good project management.  
Start small. Keep your project organised. Make it playable before making it pretty. And document what you’re doing so you don’t lose track of your own vision.

replies.author: BotherResponsible378
replies.body:
Right. I think it's easy to get excited by the idea of what AI can do and then ended up turning out what amounts to whatever one calls slop. Because when people do that it is slop. 

But what you basically described in your post is " remember when you're using AI to make a game, you should still follow the process required to make a game"

It feels ludicrous that you need to say it, but you really do. Gaming should always start with a plan. You should always map out what you're going to do and learn to pivot as you're working. That's true of not just gaming. That's true of pretty much any kind of technical project that you're ever going to work on in your entire life.

replies.author: BotherResponsible378
replies.body:
I think what happened, is that a lot of people who've never made a game or anything like that, have convinced themselves that whatever idea that they think is fun in their head is actually brilliant and that all it takes to make a game is asking an AI to just make it for you. More or less. 

People who actually know what you need to do to make a game. Understand that it's a lot more complicated than that. Even with AI. An idea that you like does not make a good game. And AI can't make an idea into a good game on its own.

Going through the process and cultivating that idea into something good is what makes a game a good game.

comments.author: Accurate-Bear7198
comments.body:
When it comes to starting out, you need to do this in the beginning especially when using agents:

1. Set up your mcp servers - these help the ai utilize and understand your software (i use it for godot and blender)

2. Modularize your code. Make it easy for ai to track down and find exact things it needs, good folder structure, naming conventions and [instructions.md](http://instructions.md) 

3. Dont have it do absolutely EVERYTHING, have it build the tools you need. For example,its not good at knowing what sounds to use, you need to figure this out. Have it create a sound studio with the animations so you can adjust sounds being used, length of the sounds, and you can even make it allow adjusting the animations at the same time

4. Create your own assets using tripo (the best ai for assets/humanoid rigging), have gemini or something get the concept, paste in the image and make it that way.

5. BUY THE ANIMATIONS. Go online, buy the animation pack you need for a couple hundred bucks and call it a day - you're NEVER going to get the animations you want with ai, it sucks ass so just bite the bullet and buy it. There is so many free animations/props online for cheap as well, so just go for it.

comments.author: Desperate_Horror
comments.body:
I've just started this journey, game development plus AI and you make some pretty good points. From my point of view the first thing I do is write my idea down, markdown in a github repository. I try to flesh it out as much as I can and as it turns out I'm kind of bad at the details. So I then get Claude to review the document and tell me what I can do better, what is missing, etc. It turns out writing down that you need about 100 experience for level 1->2 does not help anyone. What do you means, "What are the win conditions?", "What are the lose conditions?" and do "I need an endgame?" I mean it's obvious that all that stuff is floating around in my head, but if it isn't written down it might as well not exist.
 Then there is more Q&A to refine the document further. You need to keep reading the document to make sure it meets with your vision. 

Once it is written, commit it to the repo and add a CLAUDE.md the first line of which being that it is never allowed to change the document or commit it without permission.  After that I get AI to generate a list of milestones/phases and let it break down to work into bite size pieces. More reading and correcting as needed.

The first step should always be a gameplay prototype of the game loop. If the loop isn't fun you need to figure out how to fix it. Spitball ideas with AI and make new prototype. Throw away everything and come up with a new idea if needed. The point is to fail fast.

If the loop feels fun, then you get to build pieces according to the plan and then test, test and test. Give feedback and be prepared to cut things that aren't fun.

comments.author: Alarming_Turnover578
comments.body:
I would also apply your 4 point to your 2 point. Keeping everything in one big document is a good way to get AI confused as project grows. It is better to have structured plan in one document, completed features and historic data in another, overall design in third one, agent's own notes in fourth one, instructions for tools and scripts in fifth, rules in zero's one, etc.

With roadmap initially including list of big phases without much detail. And then each phase getting detailed subgoals once it becomes current. And then later those subgoals moving to history doc once phase is complete (including testing, verification by AI and confirmation by user)

Keeping everything in different files with references to relevant parts in other files and moving old information into separate history file helps AI to understands project without rereading everything. Keeping context small and clean. It not only saves tokens, but also makes agent more focused.

If game is suffiently big it also helps to list all game systems and assign tags to them, then mark relevant parts of docs with these tags to further reduce unnecessary reads.
